title: ENG-205 Early 17th Century (1603-1660) — 4 Examples (works, people, events)
subject: ENG-205

cards.def: James I's elegant, diplomatic Bible translation, which immediately became the standard English Bible.
Catholics packed a cellar beside the Houses of Parliament with gunpowder to wipe out the ruling class at a single blast.
Jonson's folio of his poems, plays, and masques, which a mocking epigram teased: "What others call a play, you call a work."
A Donne poem with an unusual analogy: "The phoenix riddle hath more wit / By us: we two being one, are it."
Samuel Johnson said that in Donne's poetry "the most heterogeneous ideas are yoked by violence together."
Herbert left a privileged position to be a rural Anglican priest, burned his secular verse, and left his religious verse to be published after his death.
The prose essay, invented by Montaigne, reached English translation in 1603 and influenced Francis Bacon and Sir Thomas Browne.
A royal book prescribing holiday festivities and Sunday sports, reissued by Charles I to Puritan anger.
Thomas Hobbes's defense of absolute sovereignty based on a social contract, written in exile in Paris.
Milton's argument against pre-publication press censorship and for toleration of most Protestants, though not Catholics.
Milton's epic in blank verse telling of the Creation and man's fall and expulsion from Eden.
A funeral elegy rejecting the Cavalier poet who would "sport with Amaryllis in the shade" and denouncing the corrupt clergy.
Royalist women writers, Philips circulating poems in Wales and Cavendish publishing lyrics after returning from Paris in 1653.
A republican memoir writer and the first person to translate Lucretius's De Rerum Natura into English.
A collection by a Cavalier poet of the Tribe of Ben.
The PowerPoint notes Charles was executed for treason by a 68-67 vote.
